ROOT = next(

    if (p / "outputs" / "measures.csv").exists()
)
OUT = ROOT / "outputs"
m = pd.read_csv(OUT / "measures.csv")
s = pd.read_csv(OUT / "scores.csv")
cal = pd.read_csv(OUT / "calibration.csv")
lr = pd.read_csv(OUT / "longrun_points.csv")
seed_fan = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "tests" / "fixtures" / "seed" / "spf_nextyear_consensus.csv")

# Panorama tables. Every summary stated in this manuscript reads one of these,
# so the prose cannot drift from the pipeline. They are written by
# scripts/build_panorama.py from src/expectations/panorama.py, whose
# docstring records the sample, balancing and skill conventions.
PANORAMA = ("1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "5_clusters", "6", "7", "7_gain", "8", "9", "10")
pan = {name: pd.read_csv(OUT / f"panorama_{name}.csv") for name in PANORAMA}
p1 = pan["1"].set_index(["survey", "variable"]).sort_index()
p2 = pan["2"].set_index(["survey", "variable"]).sort_index()
p3 = pan["3"].set_index(["survey", "variable", "horizon_key"]).sort_index()
p5 = pan["5"].set_index(["survey", "variable", "sample"]).sort_index()
p6 = pan["6"].set_index(["survey", "variable", "horizon_key"]).sort_index()
p7 = pan["7"].set_index(["survey", "variable"]).sort_index()


def table(headers, rows):
    """Render a Markdown table so Quarto keeps it in both HTML and PDF."""
    head = "| " + " | ".join(headers) + " |"
    rule = "|" + "|".join(["---"] * len(headers)) + "|"
    body = "\n".join("| " + " | ".join(map(str, row)) + " |" for row in rows)
    display(Markdown("\n".join([head, rule, body])))


def num(value, digits=2):
    return f"{value:.{digits}f}"


def pct(value, digits=0):
    return f"{abs(value):.{digits}f}"


def arrow(early, late, digits=1):
    return f"{num(early, digits)} \u2192 {num(late, digits)}"


# US next-year growth, Q1 rounds (the seed-validated series).
g = m[
    (m.survey == "us") & (m.variable == "PRGDP") & (m.quarter == 1)
    & (m.horizon_class == "next_year") & (m.year >= 1992)
].set_index("year")
tot = g.total_sd
pre = tot.loc[1992:2020]
dec_1019 = tot.loc[2010:2019].mean()
dec_2024 = tot.loc[2020:2024].mean()

# Coverage: Q1 next-year US growth.
cg = cal[
    (cal.survey == "us") & (cal.variable == "PRGDP") & (cal.quarter == 1)
    & (cal.horizon_class == "next_year")
]
cov = cg.inside_1sd.mean()
cov_row = p5.loc[("us", "PRGDP", "Q1 next year")]

# The 2026 pair: across-forecaster spread of density means (next year) against
# the ten-year point forecasts. Both are cross-sectional spreads of central
# tendencies (disagreement), not predictive intervals.
ny26 = seed_fan[seed_fan.t == 2026].iloc[0]
iqr_ny = ny26.p75 - ny26.p25
rg10 = lr[(lr.variable == "RGDP10") & (lr.year == 2026)].iloc[0]

# Longest run of consecutive missed target years in the Q1 next-year series,
# the series the coverage sentence describes.
missed = sorted((cg.loc[~cg.inside_1sd.astype(bool), "year"] + 1).astype(int))
best_run, run_start = (0, None, None), None
for i, year in enumerate(missed):
    if i == 0 or year != missed[i - 1] + 1:
        run_start = year
    if year - run_start + 1 > best_run[0]:
        best_run = (year - run_start + 1, run_start, year)
WORDS = {2: "two", 3: "three", 4: "four", 5: "five", 6: "six", 7: "seven", 8: "eight"}

# Proper scores. Skill is the ratio-of-means definition; the pooling gain is
# the same ratio applied to the average individual forecaster.
crps_gain = 100 * (1 - s.crps_pooled.mean() / s.crps_individual_mean.mean())
gain_cells = pan["7_gain"].gain_pct
gauss_losers = p7[p7.skill_pct_gaussian < 0]
ecb_coverage = pan["5"]
ecb_coverage = ecb_coverage[

inflation_tails = inflation_tails[
    (inflation_tails.window == "2020\u201322")
    & inflation_tails.variable.isin(["PRPGDP", "PRCCPI", "PRCPCE", "hicp", "hicpx"])
].ratio_95_over_05

lt = p6.loc[("ecb", "hicp", "longer_term")]
roll = p6.loc[("ecb", "hicp", "rolling_1y")]

# Report order for the panorama tables: US variables, then euro area.
ORDER = [
    ("us", "PRGDP"),
    ("us", "PRPGDP"),
    ("us", "PRUNEMP"),
    ("us", "PRCCPI"),
    ("us", "PRCPCE"),
    ("ecb", "hicp"),
    ("ecb", "hicpx"),
    ("ecb", "rgdp"),
    ("ecb", "unemp"),
]

v = dict(
    t1992=num(tot.loc[1992]),
    mean_1992_2020=num(pre.mean()),
    t2021=num(tot.loc[2021]),
    t2026=num(tot.loc[2026]),
    dec_1019=num(dec_1019),
    dec_2024=num(dec_2024),
    cov_pct=num(100 * cov, 1),
    cov_n=f"{int(cg.inside_1sd.sum())} of {len(cg)}",
    cov_years=str(int(cov_row.last_event_year - cov_row.first_event_year + 1)),
    cov_span=f"{int(cov_row.first_event_year)}\u2013{int(cov_row.last_event_year)}",
    iqr_ny=num(iqr_ny, 1),
    iqr_10y=num(rg10.iqr, 1),
    med_10y=num(rg10["median"], 1),
    med_ny=num(ny26["median"], 1),
    iqr_ny_pooled=num(g.loc[2026, "iqr"], 1),
    sh_usgdp=num(p2.loc[("us", "PRGDP"), "median"], 0),
    sh_hicp=num(p2.loc[("ecb", "hicp"), "median"], 0),
    sh_ecbgdp=num(p2.loc[("ecb", "rgdp"), "median"], 0),
    sh_usccpi=num(p2.loc[("us", "PRCCPI"), "median"], 0),
    sh_uscpce=num(p2.loc[("us", "PRCPCE"), "median"], 0),
    sh_growth_lo=num(

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Professional forecasters state their own uncertainty four times a year. Since
1968 the US Survey of Professional Forecasters has collected probability
distributions — not just point forecasts — for output growth and inflation,
and the ECB's survey has done the same for the euro area since 1999. We pool
every reported histogram by the law of total variance, decomposing total
uncertainty into the average forecaster's stated uncertainty and the
disagreement between forecasters, for every variable, horizon, and survey
round — `{python} v['n_measures']` round-target distributions. Five findings
organize the panorama. Stated growth uncertainty is stable: its pandemic
spike decayed by 2026 on both continents, while euro-area inflation
uncertainty remains `{python} v['hicp_gap_1019']`% above its
2010–19 average. Disagreement — the
only uncertainty visible in point-forecast data — is the minority share
everywhere: a median `{python} v['sh_growth_lo']`–`{python} v['sh_growth_hi']`% of
total variance for growth, at most `{python} v['sh_max']`% for any variable. Stated uncertainty stops rising with horizon by year two. Past year
three in the US and year five in the euro area, no survey elicits a
distribution at all: the ten-year questions collect point forecasts, and
their spread measures how much forecasters agree, which says nothing about
how sure any of them is.
The US distributions are roughly calibrated on average
(`{python} v['cov_pct']`% one-sigma coverage over `{python} v['cov_years']` years); the euro
area's are overconfident; both fail in clusters at regime shifts, in the
tail the regime moved toward. Scored properly, the densities beat
climatology everywhere and roughly tie a Gaussian built from the consensus
and its own error history (`{python} v['gauss_lo']`% to
+`{python} v['gauss_hi']`% CRPS skill). Density elicitation stops three to five
years out. Published estimates of AI's growth effects span roughly 0.1 to
30 percentage points a year [@shenk2026; @cunningham2025] at the horizons
no survey asks about, and we show what asking would take. A live
interactive tracks every series.

## Introduction

In the first quarter of 2026, the forecasters in the US Survey of
Professional Forecasters put a median of `{python} v['med_ny']`% on next
year's real GDP growth, and they said how sure they were: the middle half
of their pooled probability distribution spans `{python} v['iqr_ny_pooled']`
points. Asked about average growth over the next ten years, the same panel
gave a median of `{python} v['med_10y']`% and nothing else. The survey
collects no distribution for the decade. The ten-year answers sit within
`{python} v['iqr_10y']` points of each other, which shows that the
forecasters agree, and agreement is a different quantity from confidence.
The histograms stop three years out.

That gap matters more now than at any point in the surveys' history.
Published estimates of what artificial intelligence will do to growth over
roughly the coming decade run from under 0.1 percentage points a year
[@acemoglu2024] through 1.5 points [@briggsKodnani2023] — with a
0.07–1.24-point spread inside a single framework [@aghionBunel2024] — to
above 30 points [@davidson2021; @erdilBesiroglu2023]. Compilations put the
full published range at roughly 0.1–30 points a year, almost entirely as
point estimates [@shenk2026; @cunningham2025]. The one large elicitation,
run by the Forecasting Research Institute with the Federal Reserve Bank of
Chicago, collected medians and two quantiles, once [@karger2026]. The
instruments that would discipline this debate — surveys that make
professionals state distributions and then score them — exist, run
quarterly, and have five decades of track record. They stop at year three
in the US and year five in the euro area.

This paper assembles that track record in full. We compute one
construction — the law-of-total-variance decomposition of pooled survey
histograms [@wallis2005; @boeroSmithWallis2008] — for every density
variable, every horizon, and every round of the two long-running
professional surveys, `{python} v['n_measures']` round-target
distributions in all, and evaluate every one against realized outcomes
where a verified realization concept exists (`{python} v['n_cal']`
forecast-outcome pairs). The distinction we track back to 1968 is
Zarnowitz and Lambros's [-@zarnowitzLambros1987]: *disagreement* — the
spread between forecasters' means — is not *uncertainty* — the spread each
forecaster reports around their own mean.

## The elicitation landscape

Two surveys regularly ask professional forecasters for probability
distributions over macroeconomic outcomes. The US SPF has collected
histograms since 1968Q4 — for nominal GNP growth at first, real GNP from
1981Q3, real GDP from 1992Q1 — for output growth and the GDP price index
throughout, joined by fourth-quarter-over-fourth-quarter core CPI and core
PCE inflation in 2007Q1 and the unemployment rate in 2009Q2
[@spfDocumentation2026]. Density horizons ran to the next calendar year
until 2009Q2 and to three years out since. The ten-year variables — real
GDP growth, CPI, PCE — are point forecasts only. The ECB SPF has run
quarterly since 1999Q1: densities for HICP inflation, real GDP growth, and
unemployment (core HICP since 2017Q1) at current-year through
year-after-next calendar targets, rolling one- and two-year horizons, and
a longer-term calendar year four years ahead in Q1/Q2 rounds and five
ahead in Q3/Q4 [@garcia2003; @allayioti2024].

The rest of the survey landscape collects points. The NY Fed's consumer
survey elicits household densities to three years; Consensus Economics
elicits by-range probabilities at one year and publishes its 5–10-year
forecasts as points; Livingston (since 1946) and Blue Chip are point
products; the FOMC's projections come with fan charts built from
historical errors, not elicited beliefs. The two long-horizon precedents
are one-off quantile elicitations [@christensenGillinghamNordhaus2018;
@karger2026]. No survey anywhere regularly elicits probability
distributions over ten-year-ahead growth.

## Measures

Each forecaster attaches probabilities to bins. We spread each bin's mass
uniformly inside the bin, give open tails the width of the adjacent bin,
keep responses whose probabilities lie between 0 and 100 and sum to within
two points of 100, and renormalize. Moments, quantiles, and scores all use
this one distribution, so a respondent's variance carries the within-bin
term $w_b^2/12$, and disagreement is the population variance across
respondent means — the pooled mixture's variance then equals the two parts
exactly. For forecaster $i$, the histogram yields a mean $m_i$ and a
variance $v_i$. The law of total variance splits the pooled mixture
[@wallis2005]:

$$\text{total variance} = \mathbb{E}[v_i] + \operatorname{Var}(m_i).$$

The first term is the average uncertainty forecasters state individually;
the second is disagreement, the only term visible in point-forecast data
[@zarnowitzLambros1987; @lahiriSheng2010]. We report the square roots, the
between share, and quantiles of the pooled mixture. The interquartile
range of the mixture doubles as a robustness measure: bin-scheme changes
move midpoint-based SDs mechanically [@shojaSoofi2017;
@knuppelPavlova2026], and the 2020Q2 US bin widening is the worked
example (@tbl-bins).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bins
#| tbl-cap: "The wide-bin era, averaging every round and horizon in each window equally, and the clean 2024Q1-to-Q2 scheme boundary at the next-year horizon. Moments move further than the pooled IQR, which is the signature of coarser bins rather than of belief alone."
rows = []
for r in pan["10"].itertuples():
    rows.append(
        [
            r.label,
            r.period,
            r.n_rounds,
            num(r.within_sd, 3),
            num(r.total_sd, 3),
            num(r.iqr, 3),
            num(r.total_over_iqr, 3),
        ]
    )
table(
    ["Variable", "Window", "Rounds", "Within SD", "Total SD", "Pooled IQR", "Total/IQR"],
    rows,
)
```

Targets are calendar years, so a "next year" forecast made in Q1 and one
made in Q4 differ in horizon by three quarters [@ganicsRossiSekhposyan2024].
We treat round-target pairs explicitly and show the within-year shrinkage —
current-year uncertainty falls
`{python} v['shrink_lo']`–`{python} v['shrink_hi']`% from Q1 to Q4, depending
on the variable (@tbl-shrinkage) — rather than averaging over it [@clementsRichTracy2025].

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shrinkage
#| tbl-cap: "Mean current-year total SD by survey quarter, 2010-19 rounds. The fixed calendar event arrives whatever the round, so the fall from Q1 to Q4 is the value of one year of information."
rows = []
for key in ORDER:
    r = pan["4"].set_index(["survey", "variable"]).loc[key]
    rows.append(
        [
            r.label,
            num(r.total_sd_q1, 3),
            num(r.total_sd_q2, 3),
            num(r.total_sd_q3, 3),
            num(r.total_sd_q4, 3),
            f"-{pct(r.pct_change_q1_q4, 1)}%",
        ]
    )
table(["Variable", "Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q1 to Q4"], rows)
```

Coverage rates test the density at two thresholds; proper scores evaluate
all of it [@gneitingRaftery2007; @boeroSmithWallis2011]. The pooled CDF is
piecewise linear, so the continuous ranked probability score has an exact
closed form, and pinball losses at the published quantile levels decompose
it by tail. We score every calibrated round against two no-lookahead
benchmarks — expanding-window climatology and a Gaussian centered on the
consensus with historical-error RMSE — and against the average individual
forecaster. One structural note: the pooled CDF is the mean of individual
CDFs and the CRPS is convex in the CDF, so the pool beats the average
individual on every observation by construction; the empirical content is
the size of that gain (`{python} v['crps_gain']`% on average,
`{python} v['gain_lo']`–`{python} v['gain_hi']`% by cell) and where it thins.

## Five stylized facts

::: {.callout-note title="Draft note"}
Each fact still wants a figure. Every inline value and table below computes
at render from `outputs/panorama_*.csv`, including the balanced-sample term
structure and the post-2021 ECB comparison.

**Stated growth uncertainty is stable — and its pandemic spike decayed on
both continents, while euro-area inflation uncertainty has not come
home.** The pooled SD of next-year US growth was `{python} v['t1992']`
points in 1992 and averaged `{python} v['mean_1992_2020']` through 2020;
it peaked at `{python} v['t2021']` in 2021 and stands at
`{python} v['t2026']` in 2026 (decade means: `{python} v['dec_1019']`
over 2010–19, `{python} v['dec_2024']` over 2020–24). Euro-area growth
uncertainty spiked higher and decayed as fast. Euro-area inflation
uncertainty did not: the one-year series remains
`{python} v['hicp_gap']`% above its pre-2021 level in 2026 (@tbl-stability).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stability
#| tbl-cap: "Total SD of the headline series: US Q1 next-calendar-year rounds, and for the ECB the annual mean of the quarterly rolling-one-year rounds. US real GDP and GDP prices use the 1992 onward real-GDP sample."
rows = []
for key in ORDER:
    r = p1.loc[key]
    rows.append(
        [
            r.label,
            f"{r.first_year}-{r.last_year}",
            num(r.mean_through_2020, 3),
            num(r.mean_2010_2019, 3),
            num(r.mean_2020_2024, 3),
            f"{num(r.peak_value, 3)} ({r.peak_year})",
            num(r.value_2026, 3),
        ]
    )
table(
    ["Series", "Years", "Through 2020", "2010-19", "2020-24", "Peak", "2026"],
    rows,
)
```

**Disagreement is the minority share everywhere, but not uniformly.** The
median between share is about a sixth for growth
(US `{python} v['sh_usgdp']`%, euro area `{python} v['sh_ecbgdp']`%) and
euro-area prices (`{python} v['sh_hicp']`%), and a quarter to a third for
unemployment and the US inflation densities
(core CPI `{python} v['sh_usccpi']`%, core PCE `{python} v['sh_uscpce']`%;
@tbl-disagreement). The spread visible in point forecasts understates stated
uncertainty by a median factor of
`{python} v['ratio_lo']` to `{python} v['ratio_hi']` across the whole panorama [@richTracy2010;
@giordaniSoderlind2003].

```{python}
#| label: tbl-disagreement
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of the between-forecaster share of total variance across round-targets, in percent. The last column is the median ratio of pooled total SD to disagreement SD: the factor by which point-forecast spread understates stated uncertainty."
rows = []
for key in ORDER:
    r = p2.loc[key]
    rows.append(
        [
            r.label,
            int(r.n_rounds),
            num(r.decile_10, 1),
            num(r.decile_50, 1),
            num(r.decile_90, 1),
            num(r.share_at_or_below_20, 1),
            num(r.median_total_over_disagreement, 2),
        ]
    )
table(
    [
        "Series",
        "Round-targets",
        "1st decile",
        "Median",
        "9th decile",
        "At or below 20%",
        "Total/disagreement",
    ],
    rows,
)
```

**Stated uncertainty rises with horizon only until year two — then
plateaus, and for growth it inverts.** US growth within-SD climbs from the
current year to two years out (`{python} v['prgdp_h2']`), then gains
`{python} v['prgdp_h3_gain']` at three (`{python} v['prgdp_h3']`). In the
euro area, total growth uncertainty is mildly higher at the one-year rolling
horizon (`{python} v['ecb_roll1_total']`) than at the four-to-five-year
horizon (`{python} v['ecb_lt_total']`). Only unemployment keeps steepening
(@tbl-term, @tbl-term-ecb). Past year three the US record stops. The
ten-year questions collect point forecasts; their interquartile range
(`{python} v['iqr_10y']` points in 2026) measures agreement among
forecasters, and no density stands behind it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-term
#| tbl-cap: "US balanced Q1 term structure, `within SD/total SD` by horizon in years, over the Q1 window in brackets. Each window keeps only the rounds carrying every horizon it offers, so no cell is an average over a different set of rounds than its neighbour."
rows = []
for key in [("us", v_) for v_ in ("PRGDP", "PRUNEMP", "PRPGDP", "PRCCPI", "PRCPCE")]:
    cell = p3.loc[key]
    window = cell["sample"].iloc[0].removeprefix("Q1 ")
    row = [f"{cell.label.iloc[0]} ({window})", int(cell.n_rounds.iloc[0])]
    for horizon in ("h0", "h1", "h2", "h3"):
        if horizon in cell.index:
            row.append(
                f"{num(cell.loc[horizon, 'within_sd'], 3)}/"
                f"{num(cell.loc[horizon, 'total_sd'], 3)}"
            )
        else:
            row.append("--")
    rows.append(row)
table(["Variable", "Rounds", "h=0", "h=1", "h=2", "h=3"], rows)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-term-ecb
#| tbl-cap: "ECB round-balanced term structure, `within SD/total SD` by horizon class. Rounds enter only if they carry all three modern horizons, and duplicate early longer-term targets are averaged within the round first."
rows = []
for key in [("ecb", v_) for v_ in ("hicp", "hicpx", "rgdp", "unemp")]:
    cell = p3.loc[key]
    row = [cell.label.iloc[0], int(cell.n_rounds.iloc[0])]
    for horizon in ("rolling_1y", "rolling_2y", "longer_term"):
        row.append(
            f"{num(cell.loc[horizon, 'within_sd'], 3)}/"
            f"{num(cell.loc[horizon, 'total_sd'], 3)}"
        )
    rows.append(row)
table(["Variable", "Rounds", "Rolling 1y", "Rolling 2y", "Longer term"], rows)
```

**The US distributions are roughly calibrated on average; the euro area's
are overconfident; both fail in tails, in clusters.** A ±1σ band around
the consensus covered `{python} v['cov_n']` next-year US growth outcomes
(`{python} v['cov_pct']`%) over `{python} v['cov_span']` — textbook — but the
misses cluster: `{python} v['run_len']` straight target years
(`{python} v['run_span']`) around the late-1990s productivity boom, then
2008–09, then 2020–21. Euro-area one-sigma coverage runs
`{python} v['ecb_cov_lo']`–`{python} v['ecb_cov_hi']`% by variable
(@tbl-coverage) [@kennyKostkaMasera2014; @kennyKostkaMasera2015].
Scored properly, the densities beat climatology everywhere (US growth
+`{python} v['skill_clim_usgdp']`% CRPS skill; @tbl-skill) and roughly tie
the consensus-plus-track-record Gaussian: skill runs from
`{python} v['gauss_lo']`% to +`{python} v['gauss_hi']`%, with
`{python} v['gauss_losers']` on the losing side and US growth at
+`{python} v['skill_gauss_usgdp']`%. Most of what the elicited densities
know, the point forecast and its error history already carry, and for
several variables the sign of the comparison turns on how forecast rows are
weighted [@clements2018; @knuppelKruger2022]. The pinball decomposition puts the 2008–09 growth
losses in the lower tail and the 2020–22 inflation losses in the upper
tail by factors of `{python} v['pin_lo']` to `{python} v['pin_hi']`
(@tbl-tails).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "Interval coverage on every calibrated round-target, and on the comparable one-year rows. Forecasts of a shared outcome are correlated, so these are descriptive counts rather than tests."
rows = []
for key in ORDER:
    for sample in ("all horizons", "Q1 next year", "rolling 1y"):
        if (*key, sample) not in p5.index:
            continue
        r = p5.loc[(*key, sample)]
        rows.append(
            [
                r.label,
                sample,
                int(r.n),
                f"{int(r.inside_1sd)} ({num(r.inside_1sd_pct, 1)}%)",
                f"{int(r.inside_pooled_90)} ({num(r.inside_pooled_90_pct, 1)}%)",
                f"{int(r.first_event_year)}-{int(r.last_event_year)}",
            ]
        )
table(
    ["Series", "Sample", "n", "Inside +/-1 SD", "Inside pooled 90%", "Outcome years"],
    rows,
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-skill
#| tbl-cap: "CRPS skill against two no-lookahead benchmarks, as one minus the ratio of mean losses on matched eligible rows, with row-level mean skill as the sensitivity in brackets. The last column is the pooled distribution's gain over the average individual forecaster."
rows = []
for key in ORDER:
    r = p7.loc[key]
    rows.append(
        [
            r.label,
            int(r.n_climatology),
            f"{num(r.skill_pct_climatology, 1)}% [{num(r.row_skill_pct_climatology, 1)}%]",
            int(r.n_gaussian),
            f"{num(r.skill_pct_gaussian, 1)}% [{num(r.row_skill_pct_gaussian, 1)}%]",
            f"{num(r.gain_pct, 1)}%",
        ]
    )
table(
    [
        "Series",
        "n clim.",
        "Climatology skill",
        "n Gauss.",
        "Gaussian skill",
        "Pooling gain",
    ],
    rows,
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tails
#| tbl-cap: "Mean pinball loss at the 05 and 95 quantile levels inside each clustered-event window, pooling every calibrated horizon. A window is assigned by the realization's event year, not the forecast round."
rows = []
for r in pan["8"].itertuples():
    rows.append(
        [
            r.window,
            r.label,
            int(r.n),
            num(r.pinball_05, 3),
            num(r.pinball_95, 3),
            r.larger_tail,
        ]
    )
table(["Outcome years", "Series", "n", "Pinball 05", "Pinball 95", "Larger tail"], rows)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pit
#| tbl-cap: "Probability integral transform of the pooled distribution at the realization. Under ideal calibration each decile would hold about 10% of rows, so mass in the two extreme deciles is the underdispersion signal."
rows = []
for key in ORDER:
    r = pan["9"].set_index(["survey", "variable"]).loc[key]
    rows.append(
        [
            r.label,
            int(r.n),
            num(r.mean_pit, 3),
            num(r.decile_1, 1),
            num(r.decile_10, 1),
            num(r.share_extreme_deciles, 1),
        ]
    )
table(
    ["Series", "n", "Mean PIT", "Lowest decile", "Highest decile", "Both extremes"],
    rows,
)
```

**The euro area asks the question the US doesn't — and after 2021 the
long answer moved less than the short one, but it moved.** The ECB
longer-term density's total SD rose about `{python} v['lt_sd_pct']`% after
2021, against `{python} v['roll_sd_pct']`% at one year; its consensus moved
from `{python} v['lt_cons_early']`% to `{python} v['lt_cons_late']`% while the
one-year consensus moved from `{python} v['roll_cons_early']`% to
`{python} v['roll_cons_late']`% [@gornickaMeyler2022;
@deVincentHumphreys2019]. Stated long-run uncertainty peaked at
`{python} v['lt_high']` in `{python} v['lt_high_year']` and stands at
`{python} v['lt_2026']` in 2026, still well above its pre-2021 level, at the
horizon where the US elicits nothing (@tbl-longterm).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-longterm
#| tbl-cap: "ECB one-year and longer-term uncertainty and consensus, through 2020 against 2021-26. Both horizons are read from the same round-balanced panel, so neither change is averaged over a different set of rounds."
rows = []
for r in pan["6"].itertuples():
    rows.append(
        [
            r.label,
            "Rolling 1y" if r.horizon_key == "rolling_1y" else "Longer term",
            arrow(r.total_sd_through_2020, r.total_sd_2021_2026, 3),
            f"{'+' if r.pct_change_total_sd >= 0 else '-'}{pct(r.pct_change_total_sd, 1)}%",
            arrow(r.consensus_through_2020, r.consensus_2021_2026, 2),
            f"{num(r.series_high_total_sd, 3)} ({int(r.series_high_year)})",
            num(r.total_sd_2026, 3),
        ]
    )
table(
    [
        "Variable",
        "Horizon",
        "Total SD",
        "Change",
        "Consensus",
        "Series high",
        "2026",
    ],
    rows,
)
```

## The elicitation gap

::: {.callout-note title="Draft note"}
Section drafted at beat level. The argument: put the verified 0.1–30pp/yr
published range [@shenk2026; @cunningham2025] and its anchors
[@acemoglu2024; @briggsKodnani2023; @aghionBunel2024; @davidson2021;
@erdil2025gate; @korinekSuh2024] against the inventory of section 2;
@karger2026 as the one-off flagship; @chowHalperinMazlish2026 extracting
long-horizon growth beliefs from asset prices precisely because no survey
elicits them. The observation the paper owns: the instruments that would
discipline this debate exist, run quarterly, have 50 years of calibration
record — and stop at year three (US) or five (euro area).
:::

## What better elicitation would look like

::: {.callout-note title="Draft note"}
Design beats, not advocacy: extend one existing survey block to a
ten-year growth density (the ECB's longer-term question shows a panel
will answer it, and its 2023 special survey asked whether ten-year
expectations would differ [@allayioti2024]); bins wide enough to be
honest about tails (the 2020 widening as precedent [@ecbSpf2020q2]);
ship the question with the scoring rule that disciplines it — CRPS with
pinball components — because the record shows stated densities break at
regime shifts and the AI question is a regime-shift question; pair each
long-horizon density with the respondent's AI-adoption assumption so the
0.1–30 range becomes decomposable.
:::

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-note title="Draft note"}
One page: the 2026 pair again — for next year, a median and
`{python} v['iqr_ny_pooled']` points of stated spread; for the decade, a
median and no distribution — with the whole panorama behind it.
:::

## Data and limitations {.unnumbered}

All measures compute from the public microdata of the Philadelphia Fed SPF
[@spfDocumentation2026] and the ECB SPF, with bin schemes taken from each
survey's documentation for every era. Realizations are latest-vintage
[@stark2010]; real-time-vintage evaluation is future work. Forecasts of a
shared outcome are correlated, so miss counts and score comparisons are
descriptive. Benchmark windows are expanding with a ten-observation
minimum; euro-area annual histories are short. The pipeline, tests, and
every series behind the live interactive are open source at
<https://github.com/MaxGhenis/expectations>.
